title: Sequential Data
text:
Sequential Data
Why not a plain feedforward network?
Examples of ordered / sequential inputs
• Natural language: sentences, documents (tokens have order)
• Speech & audio: waveforms, spectrogram frames over time
• Time series: sensors, finance, IoT signals
• Video: frames are a sequence (often with strong temporal structure)
Core difficulty
Length may be variable; positions are not exchangeable; later steps can
depend on much earlier context.

title: Limitations of Feedforward Models on Sequences
text:
Limitations of Feedforward Models on Sequences
• Fixed-length vectorization (e.g. bag-of-words, pooling) can discard
order information.
• Treating each time step as an independent sample ignores dependencies
across time.
• Using a separate weight matrix per time step is not parameter efficient
and does not generalize to new sequence lengths.
What we want
A model that maintains a summary of the past in a hidden state and reuses
the same transition at every step (parameter sharing across time).

Batch form (conceptual)

• Many frameworks implement the step update with optimized kernels; the
mathematical object is still the same recurrence.
• Parameter count (single-layer RNN): HD + H2 + H (plus output

title: Expressiveness
text:
Expressiveness
What an RNN can represent (intuition)
• With hidden states, the model can implement finite-memory dynamics;
in theory, sufficiently large RNNs are related to finite automata / certain
sequential computations (informal bridge to theory).
• In practice, long-range dependencies are hard for vanilla RNNs due to
optimization issues (next section).
• Bidirectional RNNs process forward and backward in time and
concatenate h→
t
and h←
t
— useful when future context is available
(e.g. NL tagging), not for causal prediction tasks.

title: Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT)
text:
Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT)
Idea
Unroll the network for T steps, apply the chain rule through the graph edges
that connect ht−1 →ht.
• The loss L typically sums (or averages) contributions over time, e.g.
PT
t=1 ℓt(ˆy t, y t).
• Gradients w.r.t. W hh involve products of Jacobian factors along the
trajectory — depth grows with T.
• Truncated BPTT: limit backprop steps to a window for efficiency and
stability.

title: Vanishing and Exploding Gradients
text:
Vanishing and Exploding Gradients
Problem
Repeated multiplication by Jacobian matrices associated with the transition
can cause gradients to shrink toward zero (vanish) or grow without bound
(explode).
• Exploding: mitigated by gradient clipping (cap global norm of
gradients).
• Vanishing: harder for vanilla RNNs; motivates gated architectures
(LSTM, GRU), skip connections, or alternative sequence models.

title: Practical Training Tips (overview)
text:
Practical Training Tips (overview)
• Initialize recurrent weights carefully; use layer normalization / batch
normalization where appropriate (variants exist for RNNs).
• Learning rate and clipping are especially important for long sequences.
• For variable-length batches, mask padded positions in the loss so padding
does not contribute.

title: LSTM
text:
LSTM
Gated memory cell (sketch)
Intuition
LSTM introduces a cell state ct and gates that control what to forget, what
to write, and what to output.
• Forget gate f t: scales down parts of ct−1.
• Input gate i t and candidate ˜ct: decide what new information to add.
• Output gate ot: filters ct to produce ht.

title: LSTM
text:
LSTM
Why the cell state helps long dependencies
• Additive memory: the update ct = f t ⊙ct−1 + · · · is structurally
similar to a residual path: if f t ≈1 and the write term is small,
information in c can persist across many steps without being squashed
by the same non-linearity at every step (unlike repeated tanh in vanilla
RNN hidden dynamics).
• Adaptive forgetting: f t can learn to clear irrelevant dimensions while
keeping others, instead of a single fixed decay.
Variants (optional in courses)
Peephole connections feed ct−1 into gate activations; coupled input-forget
gates appear in some libraries. Frameworks differ in bias/layout details —
always check the doc for the exact ordering of gate equations.

title: GRU
text:
GRU
Motivation
• Combines update and reset gates so that each step interpolates
between the previous hidden state and a new proposal — no separate
cell state ct.
• Fewer parameters per layer than LSTM in typical configurations; often
similar accuracy with faster forward/backward passes on the same hidden
size.
• Used widely in NLP (e.g. encoders) and smaller models; whether GRU or
LSTM wins is task- and dataset-dependent.

title: GRU
text:
GRU
Interpretation and comparison with LSTM
• Update gate zt: if zk ≈1 for dimension k, the k-th component of h
keeps ht−1; if zk ≈0, it takes the new candidate ˜ht,k — selective
copying vs. overwriting.
• Reset gate r t: if rk ≈0, the past is ignored when forming ˜ht (useful
when recent xt should dominate); if rk ≈1, full ht−1 participates.
• LSTM vs. GRU: LSTM separates memory (ct) from output (ht)
explicitly; GRU merges into one hidden vector — simpler state, fewer
parameters, sometimes slightly less expressive for very long dependencies.
• Empirically: try both; GRU is often a strong default when training time
matters; LSTM remains a robust choice for long sequences and
structured pipelines.

text:
PyTorch
Example: many-to-one classifier
class
SeqClassifier (nn.Module):
def
__init__(self , input_dim , hidden_dim , num_classes ,
rnn_type="LSTM"):
super ().__init__ ()
RNN = {"RNN": nn.RNN , "LSTM": nn.LSTM , "GRU": nn.GRU}[
rnn_type]
self.rnn = RNN(input_dim , hidden_dim , batch_first=True
)
self.fc = nn.Linear(hidden_dim , num_classes)
def
forward(self , x):
# x: (B, T, D)
out , _ = self.rnn(x)
last = out[:, -1, :]
# take last time step
return
self.fc(last)
# logits: (B, num_classes
)
For padded batches, select the last valid time index per sequence, not always
-1.

Summary
Key takeaways
Concepts
• RNNs model sequences via a hidden state and shared transition across
time.
• Training uses BPTT; long sequences stress optimization (vanishing /
exploding gradients).
• LSTM / GRU add gating to improve memory of long-range structure.
• Frameworks provide efficient batched implementations; handle variable
lengths carefully (masking / packing).
